title: The opening of the chest
hookLine: Muslim reports that as a boy his chest was opened by angels and his heart washed

cards: Boys are playing in the open country of the Banu Sa'd. Suddenly they scatter and run, shouting to the boy's foster mother: Muhammad has been killed! The family rushes out and finds him alive, his face pale.
Something has happened to him that the other children saw only from a distance. Sahih Muslim keeps the account, from Anas ibn Malik, a companion of the Prophet ﷺ. Today: sharh as-sadr.

teach.b: Here is what Muslim reports. While the boy was playing, Jibril came to him, laid him down, and opened his chest. He took out the heart, drew out a clot from it, and said: this was the share of Satan in you.

teach.h: WASHED WITH ZAMZAM IN A GOLD BASIN.
teach.b: Then he washed the heart in a basin of gold, with the water of Zamzam, and put it back in its place.
Anas adds a small detail that brings the whole thing close: he says he used to see the mark of the stitching on the Prophet's chest.

Ibn Ishaq tells the same event in Halimah's voice, with two men in white, and says it frightened the family into taking the boy back to his mother in Mecca. So the sources differ on the details, and say so.
What does the story mean? Readers take it in different ways. Some take it as a real event that happened to his body.
Others stress what it points to: a heart prepared early, cleaned of what pulls toward harm, before anything was asked of it.

teach.h: HAVE WE NOT CAUSED THY BOSOM TO DILATE.
teach.b: Some commentators connect it with the opening of surah ninety-four, which Pickthall translates: "Have We not caused thy bosom to dilate." The Arabic there speaks of opening, or expanding, the chest.
Notice what the story does not say. It doesn't say the boy did anything to earn it. He was playing.
The washing came to him, the way water comes to a dry field. And notice the water: Zamzam, the well his grandfather found again, the water of Hajar's search.

how: Muslims know this event as sharh al-sadr, the opening of the chest; it is retold in sirah and hadith study, and some connect it with the opening of surah al-Sharh (94).

o: the well at Mecca whose water washed his heart
a gold basin kept inside the Ka'ba
the river where pilgrims bathe before prayer

s: in Muslim's report, the heart is washed with Zamzam water
in a basin of gold, then put back in its place.
the sources agree on every detail
Muslim names Jibril; Ibn Ishaq tells of two men in white.
the boy earned it by some act of devotion
he was playing with other children when it happened.

games.q: you're one of the boys playing with him. a stranger lays him down and opens his chest. what do you do?
o: run to his foster mother shouting.
games.why: Muslim reports the boys ran to his foster mother saying he'd been killed; they found him alive and pale.

practice: If there's water near you, wash your hands and face slowly; if not, do it in your mind, cool water over the wrists and palms, then cupped to your face for one breath, and let one thing you've been carrying go with it.
Muslims wash before prayer in a set order; this is not that, just a slow washing. If you pray, you can ask Allah for a clean heart in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Zamzam, the well his grandfather found again, whose water washed the boy's heart clean in the account of the opening of his chest. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the opening, or expanding, of the chest; surah 94 begins with a verb from the same root.
